Question Choices: Select. Two animals have different masses, but their masses are not given. Can comparing only the numbers 4/5 and 1/5 tell us which has greater mass: 4/5 of the first animal or 1/5 of the second? ~~Yes | No~~
Hints: You can compare the fraction numbers. To compare the resulting masses, you also need information about the whole masses.
Solution: No. The number 4/5 is greater than 1/5, but the portions use different whole masses. For whole masses 10 kg and 20 kg, the portions are 8 kg and 4 kg. For whole masses 10 kg and 50 kg, the portions are 8 kg and 10 kg. Either portion can be heavier. Different wholes do not prohibit comparison; we need enough size information.

Hints: For the same whole or equal-sized wholes, a larger positive denominator means smaller pieces. Compare the same positive number of those pieces.
Solution: Sixths are larger than eighths of the same whole. With five pieces in each, 5/6 > 5/8.

Question Choices: Amy ate 2/7 of a small muffin. Niko ate 2/7 of a larger muffin. Who ate more?
Solution: Niko. Both ate 2/7 of their own muffin. The same positive fraction of the larger muffin gives a larger amount.

Question Choices: Select, You ate 4/9 of a small chocolate. Your friend ate 4/9 of a large chocolate. Who ate more? ~~You | Your-friend~~
Solution: Your-friend. Both portions are 4/9, and the friend starts with the larger chocolate. The same positive fraction of the larger whole is larger.

Question Choices: Select. Both stores sell the same toy train and use the same regular price. Store A charges 3/4 of that price; Store B charges 3/8. Which store is cheaper? ~~Store-A | Store-B~~
Hints: For the same whole or equal-sized wholes, a larger positive denominator means smaller pieces. Compare the same positive number of those pieces.
Solution: Both stores use the same regular price. With the same numerator, eighths are smaller than fourths, so 3/8 < 3/4. Store B charges less. Select Store-B.
